scenes.heading: Comparing data sets
scenes.say: Which class did better on the test? Which player is more reliable? To compare two groups fairly, one number isn't enough. You need a centre and a spread.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Two archers: one bunched near the bullseye, one scattered all over
scenes.science: Centre = where values sit on average; spread = how bunched they are
scenes.breaks: A target is two-dimensional. Most data is just numbers on a line, and spread is the range.
scenes.say: Picture two archers. One archer's arrows are tightly bunched. The other's are scattered everywhere, but their average spot is still the bullseye. To describe each archer you need two things: where the arrows land on average, and how bunched they are. That's centre and spread.

scenes.heading: Two things to compare

left.title: Centre
points: Use median if there is an outlier

right.title: Spread
points: How far apart the values are

scenes.say: For centre, use the mean or the median. If there's an outlier, use the median. For spread, use the range: the largest value minus the smallest. A smaller range means the data is more consistent.

scenes.heading: Same mean, different spread
scenes.question: Goals in 8 games. Ana: 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9. Bree: 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10.
lines: Similar centre; Ana is more consistent
scenes.say: Ana and Bree both scored sixty-two goals in eight games, so both means are seven point seven five. Their medians are eight and eight and a half. But Ana's range is three, and Bree's is seven. They score about the same on average, but Ana is much more consistent.
scenes.caption: Ana and Bree both scored 62 goals in 8 games, so both means are 7.75. Their medians are 8 and 8.5. But Ana's range is 3, and Bree's is 7. They score about the same on average, but Ana is much more consistent.

scenes.heading: Parallel dot plots: see the spread
notes: Same scale, one plot above the other
scenes.say: Here are the same goals as parallel dot plots, on one shared scale. First Ana's dots, all bunched between six and nine. Then Bree's dots, spread out from three to ten. You can see at a glance who is more consistent.
scenes.caption: Parallel dot plots on one scale: Ana's dots are bunched from 6 to 9, Bree's are spread from 3 to 10.

scenes.heading: Back-to-back stem-and-leaf
points: Two data sets share one stem
Leaves go left for one set, right for the other
Read both sides from the stem outwards
scenes.say: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot puts two data sets on one shared stem. One set's leaves go left, the other's go right. Read both sides from the stem outwards. A seven on the left of stem one still means seventeen, not seventy-one.
scenes.caption: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot puts two data sets on one shared stem. One set's leaves go left, the other's go right. Read both sides from the stem outwards. A 7 on the left of stem 1 still means 17, not 71.

scenes.heading: Watch for outliers
scenes.question: Puzzle times (min). S: 42, 45, 45, 48, 50, 52, 95. T: 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 54, 56.
scenes.say: Group S's mean is about fifty-four minutes, and Group T's is about fifty-one. So S looks slower. But ninety-five is an outlier, and it drags S's mean up. Compare medians instead: forty-eight for S and fifty-one for T. So Group S was generally faster.
scenes.caption: Group S's mean is about 54 minutes, and Group T's is about 51. So S looks slower. But 95 is an outlier, and it drags S's mean up. Compare medians instead: 48 for S and 51 for T. So Group S was generally faster.

scenes.heading: An outlier stands out
notes: Group S: one dot far away at 95
scenes.say: On a dot plot, the outlier jumps out. Group S has six dots in the forties and fifties, and one lonely dot at ninety-five. That one dot drags the mean up, so compare the medians.
scenes.caption: Group S has one dot far away at 95. It drags the mean up, so compare medians.

points: Compare a centre AND a spread
Finish with a sentence in context
scenes.say: Recap. Always compare a centre and a spread. A smaller range means more consistent. If there's an outlier, use the median. And finish with a sentence that uses the numbers. Now try the practice questions!
